claim_evidence.anchor: Some theories of emotion seem to require belief in a real object of concern.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: This is one contested premise in a family of theories; the essay describes competing solutions.

claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Original specific experimental effect claim, not endorsed as established fact.

claim_evidence.anchor: involving seven hundred and ninety-two participants across three research groups, did not find the predicted advantage from a brief reading assignment.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Replication contrast; paper reports several conditions.

claim_evidence.anchor: involving a total of just over one thousand participants, also failed to reproduce the immediate effect in their comparisons.

claim_evidence.anchor: brought together seventy experiments and found small average cognitive benefits from reading fiction
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Small effect; moderation by comparison group and outcome; cannot claim universal empathy improvement.

claim_evidence.anchor: A later review of empathy-related studies likewise described modest, context-sensitive effects rather than a universal moral upgrade.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Literary fiction and prosocial reading combined; heterogeneous findings.

claim_evidence.anchor: greater transportation was associated with stronger story-consistent beliefs and more favorable evaluations of protagonists.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Experimental observations on absorption, belief and evaluations; limits on generalization.

claim_evidence.anchor: Aristotle, writing about poetry more than two thousand years ago, connected our pleasure in representations with learning and recognition.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Ancient argument about pleasure and imitation, not an empirical universal.

claim_evidence.anchor: Artistic excellence does not confer political authority.

description: Explores how fictional characters affect real readers without being real, using Frankenstein and Omelas to examine ethical imagination; weighs mixed evidence about fiction and empathy, narrative persuasion, AI-generated storytelling, and the value of art beyond practical benefits.
